I would suggest that that stand until Friday.

We were hoping to be able to sit this afternoon for a while at least. We have nearly finished our labours on the Bank Bill. There are some thirty-five clauses yet remaining to be dealt with. If hon. members agree, I would suggest that the njotion might be amended so as to give us leave to sit this day only and have the general question as to our sitting while the House is in session dealt with on Friday. I will bring in a new report on Friday asking for the general permission.
Are there witnesses from a distance to be examined?
No, we are through with the witnesses. We are now dealing with the clauses of the Bill.

It is intended this afternoon to take up one of the most important sections, the* interest section, and 1 should like much to be present in the committee when that is dealt with. But there are matters of great importance coming up in the House this afternoon. I know there are other members who would like to he present here, yet who would like to be in the Banking and Commerce Committee. I suppose it would be possible for us to neglect either the House or the committee, but we certainly cannot be in both places at the same time.

If there are no witnesses to be examined, but simply matters to be brought up that the committee has to consider for the preparation of its report, I cannot see any reason why the committee should not sit, as committees usually do, when the House is not in session. What reason can be advanced for this motion?

The only objection to delay is that, as I understand it, the House is shortly 'to sit in the morning, and we are very anxious, if we can, to finish with the Banking Bill before the morning sittings begin. We expect to find it extremely difficult to continue our sittings when the House has three sittings a day.
If the committees have not finished their business, that is a good reason why the House should not sit in the mornings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My impression is that
three years ago the House began sitting in the mornings quite early in the session, some time before the right hon. Prime Minuter left for England. It seems to me that after five and a half months' sitting, it is time that the House began to sit in the mornings.

That depends on the business of the House. When the budget speech has been presented and there are no more Bills to be introduced, there is no objection to morning sittings. Nobody cares to sit here much longer. 1 think I have said elsewhere that prorogation was a blessing, and I am of that opinion still. But morning sittings should commence only after all the business is before the House, and the committees have finished their work.

I desire to explain
my own position. I opposed this application in the committee. I have several amendments to move to the Bank Bill, and I did not think we should make the request to the House to be permitted to sit while the House is in session. But since coming into the House it has been intimated to me that the important matters which I had in hand would not be taken Mr. AMES.
up, and of course I have no personal objection to the committee sitting. Of course, I should like ve*y much to be there when other amendments are being considered. Yet it is very important in the interests of my constituents that I should be present in the House this afternoon, and _ so I should not be able to attend the Banking Committee.

Let it stand as a notice of motion to be taken up on Friday.

House again in Committee on the following proposed resolution-(Mr. Cochrane):
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Railways and Canals may, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council, construct, .purchase, .lease or otherwise acquire, in whole or in part, any _ railway, railway bridge, railway station, railway terminal, railway ferry or other railway work; and that any such railway or other work shall become a part of the government railway system.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
Mr. COCHRANE moved to amend the resolution by inserting after the word * work ' in the fourth line the words:
Mr. HAZEN.
For the construction, purchase, lease or acquisition of which special provision has been made by Parliament.

The minister is asking for large powers in connection with railway construction or purchase. Are there any particular railways which he wishes to purchase or which he desires to have power to construct and if so what are they ?

It is impossible to
say where railways will have to be constructed. We have had quite a discussion in this House on the question and demands for the construction of railways, particularly in Guysborough, Pictou, Cape Breton counties and also in other parts of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The lines which are to be purchased or leased is a matter for investigation. We are only taking authority to do it. If the hon. member would wait until the introduction of the Bill so that he would have a copy of it we could proceed with the discussion more intelligently.

No Bill can be
brought in except in conformity with the resolution and it would be much better for the House if the minister would be more direct and give us this information. Does it relate to the branch line Dolicv in connection with the Intercolonial?
Yes.

Why does it not so
state? In 1904 when I was minister and brought down a resolution with respect to the Canada Eastern Railway from Fredericton to Loggieville in New Brunswick
You had already purchased it?

We had entered into an arrangement. We were required to go into the most minute details. Subsequently when the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), in 1910, came to Parliament asking for authority to acquire these selfsame branch line railways, he was required to name them with particularity and indeed exception was taken to the character of his resolution because he did not give in it the full particulars. Exception was taken in 1904 to the character of the information which I laid before the House in support of that resolution which related to one particular railway. Here my hon. friend asks for power, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council:
To construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire in whole or in part any railway, &c.
Anywhere, it is not confined to branch lines of the Intercolonial, it could be in the West. It seems to me that before we come down to a discussion of this one subject of the branch lines in connection with the Intercolonial, the resolution should

state just what is in the mind of the hon. minister and the Government. My hon. fnend says that hon. members have been urging construction of this or that line. That is not relevant, that is not an answer to the objection which I make. Hon. members may desire to have certain lines constructed and other hon. member may desire to have certain branch lines acquired but the point is, what has my hon. friend in his mind in respect to the lease or purchase of these lines? If a policy has been decided upon by the Government it should be laid before Parliament and we should have particulars of the lines that it is proposed to acquire, or at least some details. It may be applied to the lines which it is intended to construct. Surely we are entitled to have that information before passing this resolution. We cannot intelligently discuss it without such information. I have asked time and again what the policy of the Government is with respect to the purchase or acquisition of those branch lines and I have been told:	Wait, wait,
you will learn of it at some time in the future. Even now, when a resolution of this far-reaching character is brought here, no information is vouchsafed to us as to any of the particulars in regard to it. I remember that in the discussion on the Canada Eastern Railway resolution the hon. member from Kings took exception to the passage of the Bill till the Government had declared their policy as regards the other branch lines in the maritime provinces or other branch lines connected with the Intercolonial, and that objection taken by him was repeated by other hon. members. They thought it the duty of the minister to say what was the policy of the Government with respect to_ other lines connecting with the Intercolonial. The minister does not indicate that this relates to the Intercolonial or any particular railway which he proposes to acquire or construct. It seems to me that he nas not been direct or frank, that them is something veiled about this. I would like to know what the policy of the Government is in regard to this. Have they in mind the acquisition of any branch lines and, if so, what branch lines have they under consideration? My hon. friend has had an official of his department, a very highly paid expert, during the past year and a half going over these railways. Surely the Government have had a report from that gentleman and surely they have considered that report and the whole question before bringing down this resolution. Or, does the minister seek to get this authority and then afterwards determine upon the policy in respect to the matter? If so, 1 do not think it is treating the House fairly. It is certainly not treating the country fairly and it .is not treating the owners of many branch lines connecting with the Intercolonial fairly. He is seeking power to expropriate any of these lines. I am
quite in accord with him if he comes before Parliament and declares frankly what his policy is and if he states that his policy is to acquire such branch lines as may be even deemed desirable among a certain number of those that will come up to a certain standard. I would heartily approve of such a proposition and I would go further, as I went in 1910 and 1911, I would support the granting of powers of expropriation, not that it may be necessary to expropriate, but that it may facilitate the acquisition of lines by arrangement. I think it is very desirable that the power of expropriation should be in the Bill. I know that in the year 1911, on the occasion when my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), then Minister of Railways and Canals, moved his resolution, I took exception to it because it did not contain powers of expropriation and because I thought it was in the interests of the country and of the Intercolonial railway that those powers should be taken by him in order that the Government might be able to gdt these roads, if possible, on fair and reasonable terms. Where the owners of the branch lines were unreasonable, it was desirable that the Government should have the power to bring them to book in the interest of the people served by these roads. I shall not refer to my remarks, which were uttered, I think, in May, 1911. But in that instance my hon. friend from South Renfrew was frank in his statement as to what he wanted to do. He was outspoken. I did not think he went far enough and I so said on that occasion. I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane), in this instance is frank with the country in regard to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is decidely frank.

He may be frank,
but not candid. He has, in remarks which he has uttered in this House, given us to understand that he does not want to acquire any branch lines and that he does not think it in the interest of the Intercolonial that they should be so acquired.
I do not think I was as frank as that.
Well, I so understood my hon. friend. Does my hon. friend repudiate that insinuation?
I repudiate the broad statement that was made. I said that I did not want to acquire some of the branch lines.

Well then, my hon.
friend wants to acquire some of them?
Yes.

Why does he not state in his resolution that he does want to acquire certain of them and that he

is coining to Parliament and asking for power to acquire some of them? Evidently my hon. friend has in his mind certain railways that he wishes to acquire.
No.
Well, I gathered that from the statement he made.
I have no particular railway in mind.

There are some lines in connection with the Intercolonial railway that he wishes to acquire and he is seeking power by this resolution, and the Bill which is to follow it, to carry out his wishes in that regard. Perhaps this is no# the occasion when this should be fully discussed, but certainly I do not wish this resolution to have even my silent approval unless I have some further information with regard to it. The course being pursued by my hon. friend is one that was condemned every year that this subject was under discussion in a concrete way. I am entirely in favour of acquiring these railways. If my hon. friend will not go as far as I would and acquire them all, then, on the principle that half a loaf is better than no bread, I would support him with respect to the acquisition of some of them at least, but I think it would be fair to this House and to the country that he should take us into his confidence as to just what he wants to do by means of this resolution, what he purposes to do and what the policy of the Government is in respect to the subject.
He has harnessed up the two propositions, although they are distinct-one, that of acquiring railways already in existence and the other, that of constructing new railways. I do not think that they should be combined in one resolution, and I think that they should be considered separately and each upon its own merits. In the matter of the acquisition of lines already in existence, I certainly think the resolution should mention those railways that the minister has * in mind, the railways which the Government have had under consideration with a view to their acquisition. I remember very distinctly the exceptions that were taken to resolutions of a similar character in previous years and the principle was propounded in this House that, before the Government should seek powers, such as are sought by this resolution, they should give the fullest possible and even detailed information. That was the principle that was supported by my hon. friends when they were sitting on this side of the House, and I think they should live up to it to-day, although they have got into the habit of not living up to any cf the principles/which they supported when in Opposition. This is a resolution which, in my judgment, should Mr. EMMERSON.
not have our approval until we have the information. I want to support any policy that will mean the acquisition of these railways and even the construction of certain others, but surely my hon. friend is not serious in coming to the House and asking for_ such general powers to construct railways. If we pass this Bill, the minister could build a railway anywhere in Canada without reference to the present Government system of railways. Surely he has no such idea in contemplation; surely he knows what railway he wishes to construct, and if so why should the information not he set forth in this resolution as it was in the resolution submitted in May, 1911? I took exception to that resolution because I thought there should be certain coal railways in Nova Scotia that should be included in it and because the terms of the resolution did not give sufficient detailed information. I am almost tempted to doubt that the Minister of Railways is in earnest with respect to the acquisition of branch lines connected with the Intercolonial railway, judging from the character of this resolution.
Is that fair?
I think that is a fair statement.
That is a pretty strong statement.
The resolution would almost lead me to believe that the Government has decided upon a different policy.

That is better; you
say 'almost' now; not altogether.

I want to be fair and I want to state the case as it appears to me from the wording of the resolution. No one reading the resolution would conclude it had reference to the acquisition of the branch lines connecting with the Intercolonial or that the minister would confine himself to the construction of railways as feeders to that line. If the minister has the intention, as he says he has, of applying this to the Intercolonial branch lines, why does he not incorporate it in the resolution? Nothing could be more indefinite and uncertain in its terms than this resolution, which asks for unreserved and unrestricted power which Parliament would be recreant to its duty if it granted.

It is much to be regretted that upon this question of acquiring the branch lines of the Intercolonial, extraneous matters should be included in the resolution, which tend to promote differences of opinion among the members in this House. On more than one occasion the House has expressed its opinion on the

desirability of the Government acquiring the branch lines and operating them as part of the Intercolonial system. Had the minister submitted a resolution simply providing for authority to lease or to purchase such branch lines on proopr terms, there would, I think, be no objection from any member of this House. We have the evidence that we are unanimously of the opinion, in the interests of the Intercolonial and in the interests of the'country, which is served by these branch lines, that they should be taken over and operated as part of the Intercolonial railway. The resolution as first submitted reads:
That it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Railways may, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council, construct, purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire, in whole or in part any railway, railway bridge, railway station, railway terminal, railway ferry, or other railway work, and that any such railway or other work shall become part of the Government railway system.
That gives a power which the minister must realize is greater than was ever given or ever thought of to be given to any minister or any government. Under that resolution, which does not seem to have been drawn with any care, the Government could commit this country to purchase a railway hundreds of miles away from the Intercolonial; it could undertake the construction of anyrailway in any part of the Dominion, and even though Parliament might not afterwards provide the money to pay the hills, the contractor could enter suit in the Exchequer Court and recover against the Government for whatever obligation the Government entered into with him. Evidently upon consideration the minister has considered it would not be desirable to press such a resolution and he proposes to amend it as follows:
To insert after the word ' work ' in line four the words for the construction, purchase, lease, or acquisition of which special provision has been made by Parliament.
Under that amendment it seems to me that the whole matter is rendered nugatory so far as immediate action is concerned. If the resolution is passed with this prohibitory clause in it, my hon. friend must still come to Parliament for authority to lease or to buy any of these branches, or to construct any new lines. That 3imply means more delay, possibly until another session of Parliament.
What would you have me put in the resolution?

I would limit it entirely to branch lines of the Intercolonial, because it is in respect of those that Parliament is already committed by a resolution just as strong as this one would be if it
were put through in this emasculated form It would simply be a declaration that this House is in favour of leasing or purchasing or building any line of railway which the Government may hereafter be authorized by Parliament to lease or to purchase or to build. It is simply an academic resolution, which gives no authority whatever to take any action. My hon. friend must see that he cannot move hand or foot if the resolution is passed with this prohibitive clause in it, because he must still come to Parliament and get this special authority. What I would do would be this: I would authorize the Governor in Council to lease for a long term of years any of the branch lines of the Intercolonial on terms to be approved by the Governor in Council, with the provision that the lease shall be submitted to Parliament at the next session after it is entered into. I am willing, and I have no doubt this House is willing, to trust the Governor in Council in regard to the leasing of the branch lines. There could not be any mistake as to that because the Government have a record of its past earnings and they could get a report of the board of management and of the engineers of the Intercolonial. If any branch lines are to be purchased, I would leave that entirely as a matter of appropriation, or I would provide in the Bill that, if it was decided to purchase any of the branch lines, a board of arbitration should be appointed by agreement to determine as to what was a reasonable price. If there was any difficulty so far as a lease was concerned, the same provision might be made. We would then be taking a step forward instead of, if this resolution were passed, being in exactly the same position as we were before.

What would you do
if we leased a line next summer? How would we operate that line unless we got an appropriation from Parliament?

That would be provided in a vote for the Intercolonial system. The minister would have to come down with his supplementary estimates, and ask Parliament to vote what additional amount he would require for that purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would bring the matter hack to the condition which my hon. friend says is useless and unworkable, namely, an appropriation in the first place by Parliament.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend found
fault a moment ago with the proposal of the minister, because he said that it all rests with the approval of the appropriation by Parliament, and therefore the minister's hands are completely tied. My hon.

friend is now suggesting exactly the same thing-an appropriation by Parliament before the minister shall act.
No. That is so far as the operation is concerned, but you must first get a lease of the road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the use of acquiring a road if you cannot operate it?

If Parliament authorized the lease, Parliament would vote the necessary appropriation to operate. The difficulty is that you cannot acquire a road; you cannot lease it; you cannot make any agreement at all under this resolution, as it is proposed to be amended. Then why pass the resolution at all? The point is that provision should be made of a definite character for the leasing or acquiring by purchase of the branch lines of the In-tetrcolonial, the leasing or purchase to be left to the Governor in Council, and provision could be made that, if the Government and the companies could not agree upon the price, it could be left to a board of arbitration, or the amount to be expended could be fixed by a referee or by the judge of the Exchequer Court, whatever might be the best way of doing it. On this resolution or on a Bill founded upon it, the minister cannot take any action. He cannot lease a road; he cannot buy one.

I could put in the
supplementary estimates an extra sum for the Intercolonial with this in view. If any road were leased this session under this Bill, we could commence to operate it and bring down the lease at the next session of Parliament for approval. I think under the resolution we can do it.

If the resolution is
passed, my hon. friend would decide what lines he would acquire; he would ask a supplementary vote for that and proceed after that to acquire the line, so that he could depend on the appropriation?
Yes.

If that ft the intention of my hon. friend, possibly it could be worked out in that way. I am anxious that we take some step forward in connection with this important matter. I would be very sorry to say a word which would hinder or delay the carrying through of the idea which my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), has contended for so long, and to which he succeeded in getting the unanimous approval of this House in a resolution passed some time ago. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways is desirous of carrying out the wish of the House. The only question is how best to do it. Although I do not agree with the mode in which he proposes to do Mr. BORDEN.
it, I would be very sorry to throw any obstacle in the way. In the province from which I come there is an exceedingly strong, and in fact intense desire that these branch lines should be taken over and operated as a part of the Intercolonial system. It is felt that the public would be very greatly benefited by that, and although for a few years these lines might not be profitable, in the final result most of them could be worked up into valuable feeders and would fee beneficial not only to the public but to the Intercolonial system as well.

Even as amended, this resolution is very broad on one point, that is, as to the location of any lines that might be leased, any new work that might be constructed or any railways or terminals that might be purchased. On looking over the resolution, I am inclined to think that one could almost, for instance, build a railway1 in connection with the Hudson Bay railway.
We are building the Hudson Bay railway.
You are doing it under a special statute.
Yes.

But I think under this
resolution a railway could be constructed not in connection with the Intercolonial or the Prince Edward Island railway at all, but in some other part of Canada. Would it fee possible, on the second reading or in Committee of the Whole, to consider an amendment to effect what is desired? This is a resolution on which the Bill is to be founded, and I understand that you cannot go very far in making amendments at this stage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It seems to me the difficulty about this amended resolution is perhaps that it ties the hands of the minister a little too much. In its original form it was probably too wide, for example, in respect to the possibility of building a road in the West which the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has mentioned. There is no idea of building a road in the West or in connection with the Hudson Bay railway under this -resolution. The minister has in mind the acquisition of certain lines in the maritime provinces, a subject which has been touched upon very often in this House, and possibly the construction of short branches of the Intercolonial railway, as I am informed by the minister, that the powers under the Railway Act for such purposes, are limited to five miles.
The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) thought this resolution was too wide without the words now proposed to

be added, which were not included in the resolution, but which form part of the Bill, and which for some reason were omitted from the resolution by the officer of the House who prepared it. Without these words the resolution certainly was of a very ample character; with these words added to it as my hon. friend from St. John suggests, it is very much restricted. I think it would be possible to work it out in the way the hon. gentleman himself suggested a little while ago, that is, to have an appropriation from Parliament at the present session enabling the .minister to proceed. As to what the hon. member for Westmorland has said concerning the desirability of indicating at the present time certain lines of railways to be acquired, I think that members of the committee will see upon consideration that that would be impossible at the present moment, because the acquisition of any particular branch line roust depend upon a certain investigation which, I think, has not been complete or has not been-

Before the hon. minister
decides upon what lines he should acquire I would like to impress upon him what I consider to be the necessity of acquiring an important branch line known as the Temiscouata road. That branch, which is seventy miles in length, extends from Riviere du Loup on the Intercolonial railway to Edmundston, N.B. I think the late Government intended to acquire the Quebec Central railway which touches the Intercolonial at Harlaka Junction, but since the late Government was turned out of power by what I consider to be an unfortunate mistake on the part of the electors, the Canadian Pacific railway leased the Quebec Central railway for a period of ninety-nine years. The intention is to continue the extension of the Quebec Cen-

tral towards Cabano on the Temiscouata. The Quebec Central railway will run to Cabano within a few years, and I think it is very important, in the interests of the Intercolonial, that the Temiscouata line should be acquired as soon as possible. For these reasons I hope the hon. minister will take action in this regard by placing an appropriation in the supplementary estimates to secure this branch line and to make of it an important feeder of the Intercolonial railway.

I desire to add a few words to the remarks made by my hon. friend and to thank him for what he has .said on behalf of the Temiscouata. That is a question

I have not given the instructions and will take the balance of what my hon. friend has said into consideration.
I beg to withdraw the present resolution and to substitute the following:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Railways and Canals may, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council, construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire, in whole or in part, any railway, railway bridge, railway station, railway terminal, railway ferry or other railway work in the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, or in any or either of the said provinces which in his opinion can more conveniently and usefully be operated as part of the government system of railways, or which may be deemed necessary or desirable for the more efficient operation of the said system.
Provided, however, that a copy of every such lease, or contract of purchase shall be laid before Parliament within one month after the execution thereof, if Parliament is then in session, or if Parliament is not then sitting within ten days after the opening of the next session thereafter.
Provided further that no such line of railway so leased, purchased or otherwise acquired shall exceed two hundred miles in length in any single instance.
Provided further that no contract for the construction of a line of railway exceeding twenty-five miles in length shall be entered into until after a sum of money for the purpose shall have been appropriated by Parliament.
Provided further that any such railway, or other work when so constructed, leased purchased or otherwise acquired shall form part of the government system of railways and shall be subject to the provisions of the Act respecting government railways and the Acts in amendment thereof.



Provided further that no such railway shall he so constructed, leased, purchased or otherwise acquired unless it directly connects with some part of the then existing system of government railways.

But it might make it
clearer because, according to the last line of the amendment, only the first one hundred miles would be admissible as there are two different railways.

speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) think that his remarks will be more relevant when we go into the estimates on this question? The matter does not seem to be strictly relevant to this Bill, although it is connected with it.

The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals stated -that he gave an answer upon this subject. What was the answer?-the matter is under consideration. The question was a very simple one. It was: Has he had an engineer on that route, or is it his intention to have that route surveyed, and, if so, when? Surely he ought to be able to answer that question particularly in view of the promise he made on the 27-th March. Let me put the question in another way: Is -the minister prepared to implement the promise which he made on the 27th March and which is found on page 6228 of ' Hansard ' ? My hon. friend f-ro-m! Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) referred -to some promise -made down there abm-t the free transportation of hay and the minister said that he -had stated in the House that the Intercolonial railway would not -carry bay free. Let me call the attention of the committee to -the -fact that -the minister did not vouchsafe

that information until three or four days after the election, in Antigonish county. When I asked the question early in December the election was pending and the answer I received was ' stands.' When the question was read from the Order Paper, the minister refused' to give the information but merely gave the answer that the question should ' stand.' But on the second sitting day after the election in Antigonish county, my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) had no difficulty at all in getting the information from the minister. What was his answer? His answer was that he had taken the ground all along that there should be no free transportation of hay on the Intercolonial railway for the county of Antigonish or the eastern counties of Nova Scotia. The minister had written letters to the late Conservative candidate in Inverness who had written him on the subject as early as October. The minister stated in those letters, the particulars of which I have received since the papers were brought down, that the Intercolonial railway was not going to carry hay free for the farmers of Eastern Nova Scotia. But why did not the minister vouchsafe that information when the questions were put to him in November and December? No, they wanted to keep these things dangling, like the supplementary and main estimates of the Minister of Public Works, before the people of the county. So it is with the promises made respecting the branch' line. The Minister of Railways says he is not responsible for the promise, and I am glad to know that the representations made by the parties down there, some of whom are Irresponsible, had no foundation in fact. The people of the South River will remember with humiliation the attempt made to fool them in this matter, as they had been fooled in the matter of public works, and free transportation of hay that were promised to that county on the eve of an election. So far as I am personally concerned, I do not mind the disrespect or contempt with which I may be treated, but my constituents have a right to be treated decently in this Parliament, and they have the right to an answer to this question: does the minister intend to have the survey made of that road and if so, when?

I answered the hon.
member when he last put the question that I did not have a survey made, and that I would take the other matter into my serious consideration.

I must
congratulate the Government on the action they have at last taken. It is now three months since we had a field day debate on the question now before the House, and the minister has no doubt realized that
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
the feeling was so general that the time had come for the taking over by the Intercolonial of many, if not all, of these branch lines, that he has at last taken action. Canada should have a Government railway system worthy of the country and one which should not be obliged to take second or third place to other railways created by this House. We have made the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk, through the generous assistance given by this Parliament, two of the leading railroads in the world, and the time has come when the Intercolonial should be placed in the same class. In Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec, there are large tracts of land which have not been developed for want of proper railway facilities. This House ha3 been generous at all times in the matter of railway subsidies, but in some places through mismanagement or extravagance or want of proper control the money has not been applied so as to give the people of these provinces the railway facilities they are entitled to. The special case I have in mind is the railway which runs through the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure, and connects western Canada with the east end of Quebec, the gateway of the St. Lawrence. Since we had the debate on this question on the 20th of January last, public opinion has been awakened in Gaspd and Bonaventure, and the municipal councils of the two counties have met at New Carlisle in conjunction with the business men of both counties regardless of party politics, and resolutions were unanimously passed asking the Government to take over the Atlantic, Quebec and Western railway and the Quebec Oriental railway. I will read a paragraph from the resolution adopted at the New Carlisle meeting, which will show the feeling of the people of these counties on this matter:
This council consider it expedient and of the most vital importance for the welfare and best interests of the coast of Gaspe that both railroads should he taken over and become a part of the Government railway system of Canada, to be operated and controlled by the same, and therefore the county council of the county of Gasp6 and the county council of the county of Bonaventure, beg to memorialize the hon. the Minister of railways and Canals to take such 6teps as he may deem necessary to acquire and place the said railway under the direct control of the Government.
Copies of this resolution were forwarded to the right hon. the Prime Minister, to the hon. Minister of Railways, to the Postmaster General, to the ex-Postmaster General who once represented the constituency, to the present representative of the county of Gaspe in this House, and to myself, as well as to the local members for these constituencies. Since then, I understand a

deputation has called upon the Prime Minister and upon the Minister of Railways, and the Rostmaster General, urging the importance of taking over this railway. I have here the latest report concerning the Atlantic, Quebec and Western railway, which shows that upon that one hundred and two miles from Gaspe Basin to New Carlisle, there has been expended $3,809,000 out of which not less than $1,114,000 was expended for the construction of bridges over these numerous large rivers that flow into the Baie de Chaleur and which are crossed by this railway. It would be unfortunate if, after an expenditure of close on $4,000,000 in the county of Gaspe, one of the oldest settled counties in this Dominion, the people should be deprived of that communication with the government railway to which they are entitled. I may recall the fact that Mr. Johnston, inspecting engineer of the Railway Department, has reported that the character of the Atlantic, Quebec and Western railway is not even second to that of the Intercolonial railway. It would be unfortunate, indeed, if this new and modern railway should be left without connection with the Intercolonial because the old Baie de Chaleur railway, which separates it from the Intercolonial railway, should be allowed to remain in the poor condition it is. The old Baie de Chaleur railway was constructed in 1884 by a company that meant well, a company which included the leading people of the district at the time together with experienced railway men, but they lacked the capital necessary to carry on such an enterprise to a successful conclusion. The subsidies were utilized more or less advantageously, but a great many complaints were made on both sides and the Baie de Chaleur railway became a football in Quebec politics for fifteen years with the net result that the people of that constituency are left with a railway which is no credit to this country. There are no fences along the road to protect the cattle, the trestles are old-time wooden trestles erected fifteen or twenty years ago, and over the Grand Cascapedia is a trestle which is patched up now and again, so that the whole railway is not in what might be called a satisfactory condition. The desire of the people is that some means should be found by the Government to take over the road, by purchase or lease or in some other way. For the information of the Minister of Railways, who is possibly not familiar with the conditions, I would mention that in 1901 the late administration gave the usual subsidy to the section from St. Charles de Caplan to New Carlisle, twenty miles, the other portion of the line being eighty miles. That subsidy was voted under conditions which were rather unusual and to which I would like to call the attention of the minister, because of the fact that there has
been so much criticism by the people in that district, that a great deal of the money had not been properly applied in the past. They insisted that proper provision should be made this time, and the control of the payment of the subsidy was left with the Minister of Railways. When this last subsidy was voted by Parliament in 1901, for that part of the line from Caplan to New Carlisle, it was agreed that the subsidy should be paid in three parts, first to the Hamilton Bridge Works Company in payment for bridges constructed in the said section of railway, and further that this was not to exceed $35,000. There was no difficulty on that score. The bridges were put up and this amount was paid. The difficulty came in on the second item for the completion of the roadbed and work in connection therewith. When the work had been completed, Mr. McLeod, who was one of the oldest and most experienced engineers of the department, was sent down to investigate the amount of work that had been done and to ascertain exactly what the trustees were entitled to. He reported that they were entitled to much less than they claimed. The Auditor General authorized a release of a payment of $114,000 to the contractors. He allowed towards the payment, under the third condition stipulated in the Subsidy Act, of overdue claims in settlement of labour, boarding house claims and materials and supplies furnished in connection with the construction of the said section of railway, a sum not exceeding $32,000. There still remained $18,000 which has never been paid out and which is claimed by the contractor, Mr. Scoles, on the one hand and by the bearers of time checks, labourers, and people living in the constituency who supplied the work, the material and the board. I advised the Minister of Railways, at the time when the part payment of $32,000 had been made, to withhold this second sum of $18,000 until, as we expected, the new Gaspe railway could take over the old Baie des Chaleurs railway. If that had been done, under the statute of 1907 they would have been obliged to pay down the sum of $50,000 for the purpose of clearing off all claim? that remained unpaid between Mata-pedia to Caplan for time checks, for board and for material furnished. It was hoped that this $50,000 that the Atlantic, Quebec and Western railway agreed to pay would wipe off all indebtedness when they took over the Baie des Chaleurs railway as well as the $18,000 of the subsidy which remained unpaid; and that both of these sums could be placed together and paid out by the minister on a report by the commissioner to be appointed for the purpose of ascertaining what claims should be recognized under this law. The $32,000 which was paid was paid on a report made by Sir Franpois Langelier, who at that time

was a judge of the Superior Court, and who was appointed commissioner for the purpose of receiving claims between Caplan and New Carlisle. The claims between Matapedia and Caplan were never taken up. We had never the means at our disposal of ascertaining exactly what the amount of the indebtedness of the company was; but, roughly speaking, from the information which we could obtain, we thought $50,000 would be a fair amount to offer to the people scattered along this coast. The Atlantic, Quebec and Western railway, although disclaiming all responsibility for these debts and claiming that they were owing by the old company, agreed, in order to put an end to the matter and to have the good feeling of the people in that district, to put up $50,000 to wipe off the whole indebtedness. Unfortunately this company went to the wall and both roads are now being operated toy trustees or receivers. Although the Gaspe railway is in first-class condition, the other railway is not; it has practically no rolling stock. I do not believe the Quebec and Oriental railway owns a single freight car. The freight cars used are almost exclusively the property of the Intercolonial and sometimes an odd Canadian Pacific or Grand Trunk car. They have a couple of passenger trains, but they are not sufficient for the needs of the country. They have lately had down there some very important companies, among them the Edwards Syndicate at Bonaventure and others from Philadelphia at Pabos, but these people have found that it is impossible for them to get proper railway communication. This railway communication can only be got by taking over these two railways and connecting them with the Intercolonial. The time has come that steps are necessary to bring about this much desired change. As the hon. minister is aware, one of the last acts of the former Minister of Railways was to have adopted in this House on the 18th of May, 1911, an amendment to the Railway Act in order to expropriate these roads, but the dissolution of Parliament in July of that year prevented this Bill from going further and it remained here. I suppose the minister saw it. It is not in the statute book but I managed to get a copy of it. It is to this effect:
Whenever it is made to appear to the minister that any railway owned by a company incorporated by the Parliament of Canada, the construction of which has been aided by a subsidy from the Government of Canada, cannot by reason of the condition of such railway or of its equipment be safely and efficiently operated, the minister may apply to the board for an order that the said railway, or its equipment, or both, shall bo put in a safe and efficient condition which order the board is hereby authorized to make after such notice to the president or manager of the company and the trustee of the bond-Mt. MARCIL.
holders, if any, as to the board seems reasonable; and the board may, by order, direct what repairs, improvements on additions shall be made to the said railway, or equipment, or both, and within what times the same shall be undertaken and completed respectively.
2. If the company fails to comply with such order of the board, the Governor in Council may, upon the recommendation of the minister, approve of such order, and direct that a copy of such order and of the order of the Governor in Council approving thereof, certified by the secretary, of the board and the clerk of the Privy Council respectively shall be filed by the minister in the office of the registrar of deeds of each county through which such railway runs, and upon such orders being so filed there shall, ipso facto, be created a first lien or mortgage upon the said railway and its equipment in favour of His Majesty for the amount of the said subsidy, which shall immediately thereupon become due and payable to His Majesty. Such lien may be enforced by His Majesty in the same manner and by the like proceedings as any other lien upon property may be enforced by His Majesty in the Exchequer Court of Canada. The said court may order such railway and its equipment to be sold to satisfy such lien, and pending such lien may appoint a receiver to manage and operate such railway. Any moneys realized from such sale may, with the consent of the purchaser, be applied by the minister under the direction of the chief engineer of Government railways towards the repair and imr provement of such railway and equipment so far as the same may be deemed necessary by the minister, and any moneys so realized, and not in the opinion of the minister required for such repairs and improvements, may be paid to the company owning the railway at the time of the sale, or to the trustee for bondholders, in the event of there being outstanding bonds secured by mortgage or otherwise upon such railway.
It was expected that that would be one of the means of bringing matters to a head. Unfortunately I have since learned that the efforts made toy the trustees for the bondholders of the Quebec and Oriental railway in England to raise money for the purpose of putting the road in a proper condition have failed completely. Therefore the road is simply kept open. Mr. Scoles has shown great energy in the matter but he is greatly handicapped. He has managed to keep the road open, but that is all. Whatever the minister does to help out the difiiculty will be gratefully received. We cannot impose our terms. What the people want is that these roads should be properly operated by the Intercolonial, because the service given by the Intercolonial under the regime of the minister has been satisfactory as far as our constituency is concerned. The putting on of the Ocean Limited all the year round has been an immense boon. Landing in that constituency at 9 a.m., is very different from landing there_ at 2 a.m., because Bonaventure is practically half way

between Halifax and Montreal. We want this railway extended through these two constituencies, and I hope that this will be done. The minister should take whatever means are required so that the legitimate grievances of the people throughout these constituencies may be investigated, and anything that is fair and reasonable should be done. Some municipalities voted thirty years ago bonuses all along the line. The hon. minister will find that in 1907 Parliament dealt with these municipalities paying these bonuses and granted them Telief on the ground that they had never received the service to which they were entitled from the company. I hope the minister will see to it that the fair claims are paid, that the relief of the municipalities who have granted in all $50,000 is maintained by being made a condition of the purchase or lease and also that the payment of the right-of-way is assured, many of the owners not having yet been paid. I could give a case at the first station out of Matapedia, at Cross Point opposite Campbellton. The line runs through land owned by a good Scotchman, M. F. Fraser. Mr. Fraser never received a red penny for the property taken away from him by the railway. The company became insolvent and he was not paid. The same is true all the way to New Richmond and elsewhere. At these places the land for the right-of-way was taken from people and promises made of payment which were never implemented, and to this day the people have received practically nothing. If one of the officers of the department were appointed as commissioner he could in a few weeks' time become familiar with the conditions there, which conditions are unusual. I hope for the sake of Canada and of this Parliament, as well as for the sake of the people concerned, that when the minister makes a bargain, he will make a good one, because the people have been complaining for twenty-five years of the way they have been treated by railroads. Some of them have been led to despair that there was any justice for them so far as railway matters are concerned. Fortunately, my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) was representing the county of Gaspe, and he took the matter up and pushed the railway to Gaspe where it reaches one of the most beautiful harbours we have in the country. I will say no more, but close with the expression of the hope that whatever the minister does will be done to give better railway facilities and remove some of the grievances which, though small matters in themselves, have been rankling in the breasts of my constituents ever since before I had the honour of being their representative, and that he. will see to it that the people get what they are entitled to. If he does this, he will do
one of the best things that could possibly be done for that county.

I wish to second the
able remarks made by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). That hon. gentleman and I have been united in our efforts to complete that railway. As stated, I have been more fortunate than he was. because we succeeded in breaking the monopoly of the old Baie des Chaleurs Railway Company early in 1900, and it was the new company that built the Gaspe section of the railway. According to the report made to the Minister of Railways and Canals bv the engineers of the department this new railway is considered as to road-bed and equipment one of the best in Canada. But while there are no overdue accounts on the last section of the railway system in the county of Gaspe, my hon. friend is right when he states that many of the peorde have not been paid for the right of way and wages in his own county of Bonaventure. Whatever arrangement is arrived at by the minister, I hope that he will see to it that those who have surrendered land for right of way or have done work for the company in the county of Bonaventure shall be paid out of the proceeds of the sale or out of the returns that are to be paid to the companv. I am glad to support what is said by my hon. friend from Bonaventure. because he has always done his best for his constituents. Unfortunately he had to face a very serious situation with the old companv. Now that the Government undertakes to relieve the people of that incubus, it is only fair that they should be paid both for right of way and for work done for the company.

I remember the field day of which the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) speaks, and particularly his own speech. I have heard a good many speeches on branch lines in this House, and none of them appealed to me to the same extent as did the one delivered by the hon. gentleman. He went into the matter not from a selfish standpoint but to give information of what there was for a road to do and what a rich part of the country it was. In reference to the position of this road, it is a pretty serious one, on account of the great expenditure that will be necessary to bring it into a safe condition. A deputation was here from the hon. gentleman's section of the country a few weeks ago in reference to the road. It would appear from the description they gave of it, that the only thing the Government could buy or rent would be the right of way. But (now the hon. gentleman tells me that even that is not paid for. I do not know what the company have to sell or lease to any great extent. The deputation told me of the very serious conditions under which the settlers and those who have business there have to labour in paying the freight

rates, and it certainly deserves the consideration of the Government and of the department, and that consideration I shall be glad to give it. I am only afraid that the terms and conditions which the company will demand will be almost prohibitive. With reference to the accounts which the hon. gentleman has spoken of as standing so long, I will undertake to have a commissioner investigate how the money is to go and as to how it should be divided.

I wish to thank the minister for the promise he has made, and I have no doubt it will be implemented at an early date. I do not wish to impose on his good nature, but there was one thing I omitted whioh I desire to mention. The deputation to whioh he refers, no doubt mentioned the bridge from Cross Point to Campbellton. There is a pressing necessity for that at this time. In 1904, this Parliament incorporated a company authorized to build a joint railway and highway bridge from Cross Point to Campbellton. This would enable the two Gaspe railways to enter; Campbellton and to connect with the Intercolonial railway eastward and westward, and through the International railway through the state of Maine with the American roads and also with the New Brunswick roads. The people of . Campbellton are very much interested in the construction of this bridge. I understood that the deputation to the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways dealt with this matter, and I have no doubt they received the assurance that it would be considered. This is one feature in connection with the taking over of the railway, a matter which I would like the minister to consider, because it will give these railways added importance from the Intercolonial railway standpoint to have the bridge built from Campbellton to Bonaventure county. It will bring these roads directly into the Intercolonial railway quarters at Campbellton, and the roads will be operated from Campbellton, which is a railway center. I see that by the resolution the minister has power to build bridges where necessary. In this case, it was to be a highway and railway bridge combined. This was in the interest of the Western railway, now called the International, which was promised a subsidy of $160,000 and also asked a guarantee of bonds. The late Government answered that unless in the case of a bridge of national importance they could not undertake to guarantee the bonds. The matter has remained in abeyance, but it is one that might be taken into consideration when the matter of acquiring these branch lines is being dealt with, because these lines will be rendered much Mr. COCHRANE.
more valuable when this bridge is built and they are brought into direct communication with Campbellton, St. John, Halh fax, the United States railways and the Canadian railway system to the West. The construction of this bridge would be an easy matter, as the water is very shallow at that point, and the bridge would not need to be more than 1,300 or 1,400 feet in length. In the last number of the Graphic, published at Campbellton, the importance of the shipments made from that point and other parts of northern New Brunswick to the United States is dealt with, and the minister will recognize the importance of this traffic when he knows that in 1912 the United States consul certified to the shipment of 922 carloads from Gloucester county and 1,517 carloads from Restigouche county, bound for the United States. So that if Gaspe and Bonaventure could be brought together by the Intercolonial railway at Campbellton by means of this bridge, this business could be doubled. Gaspe i3 three times the size of Restigouche county, and Bonaventure is larger than Gloucester county; it is an immense territory all by itself. I have no doubt that the construction of this bridge would be a good investment and it would do the people of Gaspe county the justice to which they are entitled.

It is apparent that I cannot extract very much information from the minister regarding the proposed line of railway, the interests of which I have at heart. I am not, however, dissatisfied with the information that I have received from him. We have in his statement no assumption of responsibility for the pre-election promises made in January last for the purpose of influencing the electorate, but rather a repudiation of the assurances that we got on that occasion. The minister commended the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) for giving information with regard to the line of railway he was discussing, and for approaching this subject in a proper spirit. Nothing now remains for me but to submit a few facts which not only justify but demand the building of the road to which I refer. Of course great bodies move slowly, and I am not without hope that the minister will in time see the necessity of building this road; I believe that he is more magnanimous than his curt manner would indicate. So far as this proposed line of railway is concerned, the situation is not new to the minister. I have pointed out on more than one occasion the nature of the country through which this road would run and its resources, and the minister promised on the 27th of March last that he would investigate this route, and, in fact, all routes, for the purpose of providing railway

facilities in that particular part of the country. The hon. minister on March 2, 1912, received a letter, of which I have a copy, on this very question. That letter was from the secretary of the Arisaig and Country Harbour Iron and Railway Company, Limited, and, I understand, accompanied an aplication for a subsidy for that road. The letter sets forth in such clear and succinct language the resources of that part of the country and the ease with which a road can be built that I can do no better than quote the letter. It is addressed to the minister, and, among other things, it says:
Before any decisive action is taken by you

 -
That is with regard to the construction of a line from Country Harbour Cross Roads in the western part of Guysborough county.
Before any decisive action is taken by you I venture to suggest that an exhaustive examination be made of the merits of an alternate route, viz.: that from Country Harbour Cross Roads to connect with the Intercolonial railway at the town of Antigonish.
My reasons for asking this are as follows:-
The exploration of minerals, and the development of mineral resources in that section of Nova Scotia are proceeding at a rapid rate, and for the most of them an outlet is required at the seaport of Country Harbour.
The iron deposits of Arisaig, covering about thirty miles of territory, comprise a good many beds of ore, much of it low grade, but a portion of it very high grade ore. A large sum of money has been expended the past two or three years in exploratory work, the result of which is to demonstrate the existence of ore both in quantity and quality that promises to be of great value and of economic importance to the province.
The Big Marsh Shales in the same vicinity corresponding to the celebrated Albert Shales (New Brunswick) are just now coming into prominence, in the manufacture of high-class oils. This will afford an element of traffic, as will also the plaster deposits in the vicinity of Antigonish. The most promising copper mine east of Lake Superior is situated at Poison's lake on the route of the proposed Antigonish-Country Harbour line. A large sum of money has been expended the past two or three years in sinking shafts and doing development work. This industry cannot be developed without railway connection. These four natural products would afford a traffic for a branch railway that is entirely wanting in a road from Country Harbour to Suunybrae. The former line presents no physical difficulties; the gradients are exceedingly easy; no bridging or rock-cutting is necessary, and the earth work is light. It passes through a fine agricultural country and the prospects of traffic are so good that a local company is prepared to construct and operate it if assisted with the usual government subvention, which no company has been found willing to do with the other route. This route will afford the people of Gnysborough the shortest possible connection with the
Intercolonial railway. It would be a great misfortune to the province if the Government expended a large sum of money in the construction of a railway that would fail to serve any but a small percentage of the interests at stake.
Yours verj* truly,
W. C. (Milner.
I need not elaborate on the varied resources to which the writer refers. The copper mines at Copper Lake are as he represents them to be, but unfortunately these mines cannot be properly developed, or, as a matter of fact, developed at all, unless proper transportation facilities are provided. These mines are situated at about eighteen miles from a railway, and any one will realize that it would be impossible to develop these mines without having such transportation facilities as the construction of this railway would provide. As to the gypsum deposits to which he refers, I may say that these deposits are most valuable. I quote from a report on the gypsum deposits of the maritime provinces by W. F. Jennison, made in 1911, page 61:
Although large quantities of gypsum are found in the southern and western part of the district,

The district referred to includes sections around Tracadie harbour, Pomquet harbour and Antigonish harbour.
-yet those nearest the east and northeast, particularly in the vicinity of Antigonish harbour, are much superior; in fact, it is very difficult to find exposures better 'both inquantity and quality, many of them being over one hundred feet high, some twice this height, and covering an extensive area. Much of the rock is the very best white compact, having the appearance of alabaster. It is regrettable that while the area contains practically inexhaustible quantities of gypsum of the very best quality, it is inaccessible to transportation facilities.
As to the quality of the gypsum there is no question whatever that it is equal to any that is found in Canada, and I have no doubt that, if better transportation facilities were afforded, the gypsum industry would be largely developed. Of the 5-foot seams of curly cannel, he states that ' it will yield at least forty gallons of crude oil per ton, and 15 feet of the remainder will yield at least twenty gallons '
The black shales are associated with light grey micaceous shales, with impressions of broken plants, and are in places much faulted and sometimes steeply inclined.
In view of the commercial possibilities of the oil-shale deposits which occur in large magnitude in eastern Nova Scotia, and which are referred to by Mr. Campbell in How's Mineralogy of Nova (Scotia, samples from the principal deposits were collected in both Antigonish and Pietou counties since the above was written. In fact capitalists are ready to undertake the development of these deposits if they can have some assurance or hope that railway facilities will be afforded. It is all very well to say: If you go ahead and develop your industry first we will provide the railway as soon as we find that the railway will be a profitable investment for us. That may be very good business from one point of view but I submit that in these days, when there are so many fields for investment, the converse of that should be the guiding principle for the Minister of Railways in this case. We cannot hope to get the shales and the iron ore at Arisaig and the copper at South River developed unless there is some reasonable assurance of transportation facilities. But I have not the slightest doubt that if transportation facilities were afforded the capital would be forthcoming at once. As a matter of fact there is a company now interested in the shales at Big Marsh. A company is being formed for the further development of the copper mine at Copper lake.
I do not think that in this letter which I have read anything is stated as to the character of the country and its agricultural possibilities. Through the South river valley, along the South river and all through that section is one of the finest Agricultural districts in Nova Scotia; all the way from Goshen down to South river is excellent fanning country. As pointed out in this letter, the cost of running a road through that valley would be comparatively trifling; the bridges required would be few and inexpensive, the country is practically level and there is every facility for the building of a very cheap line of railway. As to the other portion of the "road referred to, that is the portion from Merigomish to Arisaig and on to Antigonish, it again runs through a fine agrieul-
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).

*tural section and not only is there iron ore at Arisaig but it is an excellent fishing station, one of the best on Northumberland strait. I would ask, therefore, that the minister should find time to think this *matter over and at least have an engineer go over the route and make survey. As 'I have said, the minister promised in 'March, 1912, that he would have this route investigated and his attention was called to it not only by myself but by the letter of March, 1912, to which I referred. Yet at this session he says that he has done nothing to implement the promise fmade on the 27th of March, 1912, and so \ve must conclude all assurances given in January last as to the building of this road were merely pre-election promises, without foundation or justification. I say that it is up to the minister and only proper that the minister should, for the sake of his own reputation, implement the promise he made and for the sake of the *reputation of the men who spoke on behalf of the Government in January last something should be done in the way of assisting to build a line through the South River valley as a feeder to the Intercolonial *railway.

speechtext:
The harbour commissioners have made an application to us for an advance of $3,500,000 for the purpose of carrying out these harbour improvements. The figures are made up as I have stated them to my right hon. friend. In the statement submitted to us it is said that:
Messrs. Coode, Matthews, Fitzmaurice and Wilson, of London, England, made a report dated the 21st January, 1913, to the commissioners in regard to the proposed increased wharfage accommodation in the harbor, for ocean-going steamers and other large vessels. The existing accommodation, they state, is extremely limited for a port possessing such natural advantages and vast prospects of trade expansion. The provision of additional berthage and other facilities connected therewith could not fail, in their opinion, to prove of immense benefit to the port and to the country at large.
The plans submitted show the additional wharfage accommodation and reclaimed areas that could be provided. Arrangements would not, of course be made in the first instance for constructing the whole of the accommodation, at each site as shown on the drawing, but for putting in hand and executing the work in such instalments as might be considered desirable from time to time, each portion forming a section of the complete project.
The present accommodation at this point consists of the tidal basin which has an area of 18 acres, with 3,300 feet of quayage and a depth of 26 feet at low water of spring tides. The entrance to the basin is 200 feet wide.

The west dock, opening from the tidal basin, is about 2,400 feet long by 600 feet in average breadth with an area of 40 acres and a quay frontage of about 3,400 feet. The depth of water in the wet dock is from 22 to 30 feet and the depth over the sill of the gates is 35 feet at high water of spring tides. The width of the entrance from the tidal basin is 60 feet. From the north east corner of the tidal basin a pier extends northwards a distance of 1,600 feet. The pier is 300 feet in width and provision has been made for berthage on both faces, although the inner berth, 1,000 feet in length, is not as yet available pending the completion of the necessary dredging alongside and in the approach; There is a depth of over 40 feet at low water of spring tides alongside the outer face of this pier.
Large additions to the present dock facilities have been contemplated for some time past, northward of the Louise embankment. The main feature of that scheme is the construction of a large separate basin in which extensive further berthage accommodation is obtained by a system of projecting jetties, about 1,000 feet in lenght, pointing approximately north and south. The construction of pier No. 1 was the first step undertaken in the execution of those proposals, and in continuation thereof the Louise embankment has been widened on its northern face nearly as far as the root of the proposed pier No. 2 which it was intended to construct parallel with pier No. 1 and at a distance of 500 feet therefrom. The engineers do not however, favour the construction of short jetties. They are of opinion that economical advantages are afforded by providing the wharfage accommodation in one continuous line. It gives a greater amount of berthage and adapts itself to the various lengths of ships to be accommodated.
As a first instalment, the engineers recommend the widening of the Louise embankment. The basin opposite the proposed widening would ultimately be about 3,300 feet to 4,000 feet in length by 2,000 feet to 2,500 feet in width, thus affording a very large space for the maneuvering of vessels entering and departing. This basin would be dredged to a depth of 35 feet below the level of low water of ordinary spring tides. In the first instance, however, and until the 'proposed pier,' as shown on the plan was executed, it would be unnecessary to dredge the full width of the basin. This basin when completed would have an entrance width of 1,500 feet. The proposed widening of the embankment and the area of 80 acres to be reclaimed in this vicinity are shown on the plan by red colour of dark tint.
